sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: AI systems can now operate Blender, follow instructions in complex video games, and manipulate objects with robot arms. What range of physical goals can today's AI systems achieve autonomously? Answering this question requires testing systems on tasks that demand different combinations of perception, memory, planning, and action. We introduce \textbf{WorldLeague}, a benchmark that compares AI systems on a common set of \textbf{60 simulated robot tasks} by measuring progress toward each task's physical goal from the robot's trajectory. Robots explore scenes to gather evidence in \textbf{WorldSeek}, rearrange objects in \textbf{WorldShape}, and adapt to changes in \textbf{WorldShift}. Tying these goals to a single control interface limits which AI systems can be compared. In WorldLeague, vision-language models (VLMs) choose targets and motions, while vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs) use their native controls. For each of six capability dimensions, we measure how much progress a system makes toward its goals (Interactive Score) and how often it achieves them (physical success rate). Together, these measures form the system's \emph{Physical Agency Profile}. Among 13 representative AI systems, Claude Fable 5.2 achieves 13 of the 60 goals and earns the highest mean Interactive Score (28.58/100). Fable leads in four dimensions, while GPT-6.1-Sol and GPT-6-Astra tie for first on rule-following tasks. Even when VLMs answer every final question correctly, they receive an Interactive Score of zero in 71.8\% of those episodes. WorldLeague gives Embodied AI, Physical AI, and Agentic AI a shared basis for comparing what AI systems achieve autonomously, from partial progress toward a physical goal to full goal completion. Project Webpage: https://xyangzhou.github.io/WorldLeague

Corresponding author. 1. Introduction Foundation models have recently become promising direction for building general-purpose robots [39]. In digital environments, agents built on frontier models can follow instructions in open-world video games [9] and turn visual references into editable 3D scenes in Blender [53]. The range of tasks that physical robots can perform has also grown [29, 43]. Robots have performed long-horizon household tasks, such as cleaning kitchen or bedroom, in homes they had never seen during training [41]. To clean an unfamiliar kitchen, robot must use what it sees to decide what to do next. Embodied AI systems connect perception to action in different ways [61]. vision-language model (VLM) can identify an object from spatial description [16] and estimate its distance from other objects [30]. With robot interface, it can use such judgments to choose where to move or grasp [10]. Vision-language-action (VLA) models produce robot actions directly from instructions and visual observations [47]. For example, Gemini Robotics 1.5 interleaves reasoning and action during multi-step manipulation [31]. World-action models (WAMs) jointly predict future observations and robot actions [15, 32, 44, 49]. This approach has enabled closed-loop manipulation on new tasks and in new environments [52]. Across these approaches, the ambition is the same. person specifies physical goal and leaves the system to decide how to achieve it [10, 13, 17, 18, 22, 40]. We call the system making those decisions the agent and its capacity to choose and execute actions through body its physical agency. The decisions an agent must make depend on the goal. To find hidden object, it must decide where to look and what to move out of the way [3, 7, 48]. To put that object through narrow opening, it must also choose an orientation that fits. An agent may therefore find the right object and still fail to put it away. This leads us to the central question of our study. What range of physical goals can todays AI systems achieve autonomously? Organizing robot benchmarks around household activities [23, 59] obscures what success on each activity establishes about an agent. Consider robot asked to deliver cup. If the user names the cup and it is in plain sight, the robot can select it from its current view. If the user asks for the cup that has moved since the robot last visited the room, the robot must use an earlier observation to decide what to pick up. Both tasks count as cup delivery. Yet success on the first leaves the decisive requirement of the second entirely untested. To establish the range of an agents physical abilities, we must vary what the agent has to work out for itself and verify that its actions bring about the requested outcome. We introduce WorldLeague, benchmark of 60 simulated robot tasks organized by the physical demands that determine success. We evaluate VLMs, VLAs, and WAMs against shared goals and constraints. For each task, the robots trajectory shows which goal requirements it satisfies and whether it completes the task. The tasks span three tracks, each defined by what the robot must do to achieve its goal. WorldSeek tests navigation and goal grounding as systems explore and gather evidence. WorldShape tests geometric reconfiguration and physical reasoning as systems change the scene. WorldShift tests temporal memory and constraint management as systems track changing world and recover from disturbances. The three tracks span six capability dimensions (Sec. 3.1). We group each task by its primary challenge, and single task can draw on capabilities from several dimensions. To compare systems across these tasks, we instantiate each goal in scene with specified objects, initial conditions, and constraints. Physical predicates check conditions such as stable placement or recovery after disturbance. We inspect all 60 taskscene pairs, verify that reference runs meet the goals and constraints, and check the scoring conditions against the task specifications. Each system pursues its goal through physical interaction. For VLMs, our decision-preserving action abstraction draws on how sensorimotor mechanisms coordinate fine-grained human movement [12, 14, 45]. The interface executes motions, and 2 the agent chooses the targets, action parameters, sequences, and responses to feedback that shape the outcome. We adapt motion interface [10] to implement this abstraction on R1 [23]. VLA and WAM policies use their native interfaces under shared task goals, constraints, and physical scoring rules. We score the resulting trajectory for progress toward individual requirements and for physical success, which requires satisfying the full goal and all task constraints. Physical Agency Profile reports Interactive Score for progress and physical success rate for complete goal achievement in each capability dimension. For VLMs, terminal question answering (QA) provides an auxiliary measure of scene understanding, outcome recognition, and memory within the same episodes. Among the 13 evaluated embodied AI systems, Claude Fable 5.2 earns the highest overall Interactive Score, 28.58 out of 100, and achieves physical success on 13 of its 60 tasks. Fable leads in navigation, goal grounding, geometric reconfiguration, and temporal memory, while GPT-6.1-Sol and GPT-6-Astra lead in constraint management. The trajectory analysis also identifies goal requirements that remain unmet after systems make physical progress. Of 347 VLM episodes with full terminal QA credit, 249 (71.8%) receive an Interactive Score of zero. These results show that goal-relevant understanding and successful intermediate actions can coexist with unmet physical goals. Turning demonstrated capabilities into desired physical outcomes is central to Embodied AI, Physical AI, and Agentic AI, which share the ambition of building systems that can pursue human goals through their own actions in the world. WorldLeague turns this ambition into common experiment. person specifies the desired outcome, an agent determines how to pursue it through body, and the evaluation verifies what it achieves in the physical environment. Evaluating systems against common goals and physical success criteria allows advances in perception, reasoning, and control to be assessed in terms of what they enable these systems to accomplish [46]. Our broader aim is to make autonomous goal achievement shared measure of progress for AI systems that act in the world. We make three contributions to the evaluation of physical agency in embodied AI systems. We test physical agency by goal achievement on tasks with different capability combinations. We build and validate WorldLeague, suite of 60 tasks that measures progress and physical success across six capability dimensions using shared goals and scoring rules. We compare the capability profiles of 13 systems and identify goal requirements that remain unmet in episodes with correct answers or partial physical progress. 2. Related Work 2.1. The Demands of Physical Goals BEHAVIOR-1K [23] takes everyday household activities as the unit of evaluation. Within single activity, what robot must decide can change as it acts [34]. In RoboQuest [4], robot uses trial impressions to decide how to stamp the requested pattern. MeMoREval [5] makes later request depend on what the system encountered earlier, while RobotAgentBench [1] introduces disturbances that require an agent to revise an ongoing manipulation. WorldLeague organizes goals by the primary challenge they pose. Finding specified object and fitting it through narrow opening both require identifying the object, but the second goal also requires reasoning about orientation and clearance. Grouping tasks this way lets us trace how success varies across exploration, physical transformation, and adaptation. 3 2.2. Action Abstraction for Embodied AI Systems An action interface determines which decisions the agent makes [63]. SayCan [42] uses skills feasibility to guide selection, and Code as Policies [33] lets model compose robot actions in program. Inner Monologue [11] feeds execution outcomes back into planning. Show-Harness [10] translates agent-selected commands through an embodiment-specific interpreter, and HumanCLAW [25] uses the separation between action selection and motor execution to study how VLMs direct body. WorldHarness adapts Show-Harness to preserve the VLMs decisions throughout task. To place an object, the VLM chooses where to grasp, how far to move, and when to release. The controller executes the motion and returns feedback that the VLM can use to correct its next move. VLA and world-action policies pursue the same goals through their native interfaces. 2.3. Measuring Physical Goal Achievement ESI-Bench [51] lets systems move and manipulate objects to gather evidence for spatial answer. ALFRED [62] scores both task success and the fraction of goal conditions met. IMBench [35] examines understanding, planning, and execution in separate stages. WorldLeague builds on selected ESI-Bench scene records to pair what VLM can report with what it physically achieves in the same episode. Once the physical outcome is fixed, terminal QA probes the VLMs understanding of the scene and its actions. Across all three model families, Physical Agency Profiles show how partial progress and full goal achievement vary across the six dimensions. 2.4. Comparison with Existing Benchmarks Table 1 compares 17 benchmarks by the capabilities their tasks score and the actions their agents control (Appendix A.3). RoboQuest and IMBench couple active perception to manipulation by asking agents to uncover information they need to change physical configuration. MeMoREval tests whether an earlier observation guides later choice, and RobotAgentBench tests recovery under constraints. WorldLeague evaluates all six dimensions through physical goal achievement, so the same systems ability to find and manipulate target can be compared with its ability to track that target as the scene changes. 3. WorldLeague Benchmark 3.1. Physical Goals and Task Demands human specifies desired outcome and leaves the agent to decide how to bring it about. To measure the range of goals an embodied AI system can achieve this way, WorldLeague varies what the physical world demands of it. Across 60 tasks, systems explore to find the evidence goal requires, change the physical configuration of scene, and adapt as events alter what they must do next. These challenges define the tracks. WorldSeek. Where the robot goes determines what it can reach and what it can see. An ordered pickup tests spatial navigation. The robot chooses its route, visits six rooms in the prescribed order, and collects the requested items on its tray. search for hidden object tests goal grounding. The robot must decide where to look or what to move to expose the candidates, then use what it sees to identify and retrieve the requested object. WorldShape. Action Interfaces and Decision Responsibility To evaluate how VLM pursues goal, we let it choose target, motion, and response when the outcome changes its plan. Human motor control offers model for this division of responsibility. Sensorimotor feedback coordinates the fine movements needed to carry out chosen action [12, 45]. Show-Harness [10] and HumanCLAW [25] show how an embodied interface can separate action selection from motor execution. In our decision-preserving action abstraction, the VLM chooses where to grasp, how far to move, when to release, and what to try next if motion stops early. WorldHarness implements this abstraction on R1 by adapting Show-Harness  (Fig. 3)  . Given the public goal, camera observations, and retained history, the VLM selects base, arm, trunk, or gripper command. The controller executes the motion and returns feedback, which the VLM can use to revise its next command. The evaluator records the resulting physical states and task events. VLA and WAM policies use their native interfaces and trained embodiments to produce control commands or action chunks. All three model families share the task goals, constraints, and physical scoring rules. WorldLeague can therefore compare different policies, harnesses, and robots by the goals each embodied AI system achieves through its own perception, reasoning, and control. Evaluation Protocol We give 13 embodied AI systems the same physical goals and score what each achieves through its own perception and control. Eight VLMs direct R1 through WorldHarness. Three VLA and two WAM policies act through their native controllers on PandaOmron or R1Pro. Each VLM runs all 60 tasks. Each continuous-control policy runs 59 tasks, excluding T52, whose containment condition already holds at initialization. With one episode per system and task, this gives 775 episodes at seed 0. We also repeat the full suite with GPT-6.1-Sol at seed 1. Within each interface family, systems have the same task-specific interaction budgets, ranging from 10 to 342 VLM decisions or 1,000 to 40,000 control steps. Six VLMs select parameterized motions and can revisit earlier images and save notes. Gemini and Jev select command and repetition count from current views and public interaction records (Appendix C.2). We report mean Interactive Score (I, out of 100) and physical success rate (S, in percent), weighting tasks equally. Terminal QA probes the VLMs account of the same episode after its physical outcome is fixed. 4.2. On the allocation task, Sol declares completion at decision 74 with saved notes and uses all 94 decisions with notes hidden. Both runs satisfy three of four placement checks and miss different placements (Appendix D.6). 4.5. What VLMs Can Report About an Episode VLM can correctly describe an unsuccessful attempt. Of 347 VLM episodes with full terminal QA credit, 249 (71.8%) earn zero Interactive Score. The zero-credit rate across all 480 VLM episodes 11 is 76.3%. Figure 5 shows this pairing for each VLM. Appendix D.2 reports results across initialstate, final-state, and history questions. On T42, for example, Sol correctly reports that no object completed valid physical trial. T21 shows the converse. Sol builds stable tower and answers the question about the maximum-stability ordering incorrectly. Figure 5: What eight VLMs report and achieve in the same episode. Left, mean Interactive Score and terminal QA over all tasks. Right, the distribution of zero, partial, and full Interactive Scores among the episodes in which each VLM answers every question correctly. On 12 tasks, we also ask Sol the initial-state question before its first action. We keep its answer out of the control context and ask the same question again at termination. Sol answers six correctly at the start and ten at the end. Of the six it answers correctly at the start, it completes three physical goals and earns zero progress on the other three (Appendix D.6). 4.6. Variation Across Runs and Computational Cost Sols overall Interactive Score changes from 22.28 to 21.44 across two environment seeds, yet its score changes on 11 of 60 tasks. Sol builds the T21 tower only at seed 0 and completes the T46 change-guided delivery only at seed 1. These gains and losses nearly cancel in the overall score (Appendix C.1). Figure 6 compares physical progress with mean elapsed time for all 13 systems and mean token use for the eight VLMs. Gemini-Decision is at the low-resource end of both observed Pareto frontiers, and GR00T is the only continuous-control policy on the elapsed-time frontier. Fable and Qwen each take about 51 minutes per task. Fable earns the highest score, 28.58, with 3.07 million tokens per task, and Qwen earns 6.31 with 6.47 million. GR00T spends 16.39 of its 23.83 minutes per task in simulator execution and 1.08 in inference. Sol spends 14.74 of its 46.36 minutes in inference. Total elapsed time also includes observation and harness overhead (Appendix E). Across the eight VLMs, terminal QA accounts for 0.102.70% of inference time, so most model-request time is spent choosing actions during physical interaction. 12 Figure 6: Overall Interactive Score versus mean elapsed minutes per task (left, all models) and mean millions of tokens per task (right, VLMs). Both horizontal axes are logarithmic. Lines connect the observed Pareto-optimal points. Colors identify models and shapes distinguish model families. As in the physical world, the environment keeps running during model inference (Appendix C.2). The scene can therefore change between observation and action execution, making inference latency practical consideration for physical interaction. 5. Conclusion WorldLeague evaluates physical agency across 60 tasks in exploration, physical transformation, and adaptation. Across 13 models, the highest Interactive Score is 28.58 out of 100. Every VLM scores higher on auxiliary QA than on physical operation, and completed commands often leave physical goals unmet. Of the 347 VLM episodes that receive full credit for terminal QA, 249 (71.8%) receive zero operation credit for the physical task. WorldHarness traces these outcomes to the agents choice of targets and motion parameters and to its subsequent actions. The same predicates that determine the capability profile show which requirements remain unmet in each trajectory, from stable placement after release to finding and delivering the right object after scene change. The world continues to evolve while model reasons, making inference latency relevant to the evaluation of physical interaction. Future Work. We could adapt JEPA-based planners such as V-JEPA 2-AC [8] to WorldLeague to test whether action-conditioned latent predictions help with geometric reconfiguration and recovery from disturbances. For these experiments, we would use the generator in Appendix to sample template with fixed probability wi and then draw an instance from pi, yielding p(z, i) = wi pi(z). We would group instances by scene, object-role assignment, layout, and events before assigning groups to splits, retaining the 60 fixed evaluation instances as the test set. The same generator could supply screened pool for online reinforcement learning. At each reset, the environment would sample an instance from the pool, initialize the objects and robot pose, clear the episode history, and install the task events. The policy would receive the public goal, observations, and feedback through the interaction interface (Sec. 3.3), and physical progress and terminal success could serve as reward signals.

Reading the Six Capability Dimensions Table 1 marks dimension as fully covered when the benchmark scores its demands together. Partial coverage means that an explicit test measures one component. The Execution column records who controls the motions. Feedback-guided robot motion earns full mark, delegated skills, symbolic commands, and exploration for QA earn partial mark, and passive prediction has no execution mark. WorldSeek. Navigation links route or region choices to physical arrival. Arrival checks, symbolic traversal, and route questions each test component. Goal grounding links identification of the intended target to action that reveals decisive evidence [3]. Selecting visible referent tests the identification component. WorldShape. Geometric reconfiguration couples choices about shape, clearance, or orientation to an achieved arrangement. Relational placement and insertion alignment test individual components. Physical reasoning links prediction about an actions consequences to an intervention, such as stabilizing support or choosing launch. Contact predictions and material-outcome checks each test component. WorldShift. Temporal memory requires the agent to use earlier physical evidence when changed scene calls for decision. Video world models can use spatial memory to predict future frames more efficiently [19]. World-action models use predictions of future states to guide action selection [32].
